The ultimate Responsible Party is whoever bears the consequences; everyone must report to someone.
Remember the force behind the thing: specific people, not the organization, produce results.
Match the person to the design; make hiring systematic and scientific (values, then abilities, then skills).
People are built differently; different ways of thinking suit different jobs; use assessments.
Think like a sports manager: no one has everything, yet everyone must excel.
Pay attention to track records: has the person done the thing successfully at least three times?
Hire people you want to share your life with, not just to fill the first job.
Compensation should provide stability and opportunity; pay for the person; tie metrics at least loosely to pay.
In great partnerships consideration and generosity matter more than money.
Great people are hard to find; think about how to keep them.
You and the people you manage go through a process of personal evolution; careers are discovered, not planned.
Provide constant feedback.
Evaluate accurately, not kindly; people overrate their own contributions (self-reports summed to 301 percent).
Tough love is the hardest and most important kind.
Do not hide your observations about people; build the synthesis from specific dots; use evaluation tools.
Make learning what someone is like an open, evolutionary, iterative process with clear, impartial metrics.
How someone operates and whether that way works (process plus outcomes over time) matters more than any one result.
When you are truly in sync with someone about their weaknesses, they are probably true; it should take under a year to know.
Train, guardrail, or remove people; do not try to rehabilitate them.
A transfer's goal is the best, highest use of the person for the community.
Do not lower the bar.
Look down on your machine from a higher level: compare outcomes to goals; think like an organizational engineer; build great metrics.
Every case has two purposes: move toward the goal and train/test the machine; policies are extensions of principles.
Distinguish managing, micromanaging, and not managing; believability applies to management too.
Know what your people are like and what makes them tick; calibrate how much confidence to have in each.
Clearly assign responsibilities; watch for job slip.
Probe deep and hard to learn what to expect from your machine (daily updates, transparent probing, pull suspicious threads).
Think like an owner and expect the same of others.
Recognize and deal with key-man risk.
Do not treat everyone the same; treat them appropriately.
Great leadership is not what it is made out to be: do not average opinions, be weak and strong at once, seek to be understood.
Hold yourself and your people accountable; distinguish a broken contract from an unforeseen event.
Communicate the plan clearly with metrics that show whether you are on track.
Escalate when you cannot adequately handle your responsibilities and expect others to do the same.
If you are not worried, you need to worry; if you are worried, you need not.
Design and oversee a machine for perceiving whether things are good enough (assign problem-perceivers; taste the soup).
Be very specific about problems; avoid the anonymous 'we' and 'they'.
Do not be afraid to fix the difficult things; distinguish problems with planned solutions from those without.
Diagnose by asking: was the outcome good or bad; who is responsible; if bad, is the Responsible Party incapable and/or is the design bad?
Maintain an emerging synthesis by diagnosing continuously.
Diagnoses must produce outcomes: theories of root cause, data to gather, plans.
Use the drill-down technique for an 80/20 understanding of a struggling unit: list problems, root causes, plan, execute with public tracking.
Diagnosis is foundational to both progress and quality relationships.
Build your machine instead of handling cases one by one.
Systemize your principles and how they are implemented; build decision-making machines from explicit criteria.
A good plan should read like a movie script: visualize alternatives, weigh second-order effects, use standing meetings.
Design is iterative; between a bad now and a good then is a working-through-it period.
Build the organization around goals rather than tasks; top-down; manager ratios; double-do critical tasks.
Make the org chart a pyramid with straight reporting lines; cross-department issues resolve at the pyramid's point.
Create guardrails when needed, but it is better not to need them; people will not see their own blind spots.
Keep the strategic vision constant while adjusting tactics.
Have good controls so you are not exposed to dishonesty: investigate, use auditors, avoid rubber-stamping, make consequences visible.
Have the clearest possible reporting lines and delineations of responsibility; think about leverage.
Almost everything takes more time and costs more than you expect.
Work for goals you and the organization are excited about, and connect tasks to them.
Everyone has too much to do: do less, delegate, or improve productivity.
Use checklists, but checklists are not a substitute for personal responsibility.
Allow time for rest and renovation.
Celebrate completion.
Principles embedded in tools are especially valuable for an idea meritocracy: they change habits, convert data into conclusions, and make conclusions auditable by their logic and data.
All organizations must have checks and balances: merit is not the only factor in assigning authority; nobody is above the system; decision rights and vote weights explicit; assessors independent.
A single CEO is not as good as a great group of leaders.
No governance system of rules and checks can substitute for a great partnership.
